card.keepWhy: Less, on purpose, to make room.
sources: Matthew 4:1-11 and Luke 4:1-13 (after his baptism Jesus is led into the desert; fasts forty days and forty nights; is hungry; the tempter: command these stones to become bread; “Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God” (Deuteronomy 8:3); the kingdoms of the world offered if he will fall down and worship; “The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve”; the devil leaves and angels minister to him).
Genesis 3:19 (dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return); Roman Missal, Ash Wednesday: “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return” or “Repent, and believe in the Gospel.”

Catechism of the Catholic Church 540 (Lent unites the Church to the mystery of Jesus in the desert), 1434, 1438 (prayer, fasting, almsgiving; Lent as a penitential season); Code of Canon Law 1250-1253 (Fridays and Lent; abstinence from meat; fasting on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday).

Comparative note: Orthodox Christians keep Great Lent beginning on Clean Monday, without Ash Wednesday; many Anglican, Lutheran and Methodist churches also keep Ash Wednesday and Lent; many other Protestant churches do not.
check: The lesson shows two of the three temptations (bread, the kingdoms) and leaves out the temple pinnacle for length; confirm that is acceptable.
Caption order follows Matthew (kingdoms last); Luke places the temple last.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there something you reach for without even thinking? your phone, a snack, a complaint?
options: same here. hold that thought. this story is about saying no to something, on purpose.
that’s so human. this one starts with a very hungry man. listen.
fair. you don’t have to. just listen.

steps.line: After his baptism, Jesus walked alone into the desert. For forty days and nights, he ate nothing.
Cold nights, empty days, only stars and stone. When it was over, he was hungry. And the tempter came.

steps.q: He’s been starving for forty days. What do you think the first temptation is?
o: Leave the desert and go eat
Ask the angels to bring food
steps.why: Bread. The most natural thing in the world to want, right then.

steps.line: “If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.”

steps.q: Jesus answers all three temptations the same way. How?
steps.why: All three answers come from Deuteronomy, Moses’ words to Israel about their forty years in the wilderness. Many readers see it: where Israel stumbled in the desert, Jesus holds fast.

steps.line: Then he was shown all the kingdoms of the world. All of it could be his, if he would only bow down. He said no. Worship belongs to God alone.
The tempter left him. And angels came and cared for him.

steps.q: Count from Ash Wednesday to Easter and you get forty-six days. How does Lent make forty?
o: Holy Week is counted on its own
The first week is a warm-up
steps.why: Traditionally the Sundays don’t count as fast days: every Sunday is a little Easter, a feast. That leaves forty, to keep Jesus company in the desert.

steps.line: Today, Lent begins on Ash Wednesday. A cross of ash is traced on the forehead: “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
steps.label: today

steps.line: Then forty days of prayer, fasting and giving to the poor. Many give something up. And on the Fridays of Lent, no meat.
steps.label: today

steps.q: On Lent’s Fridays, beef and chicken are out, but fish is fine. What’s the usual explanation?
o: Meat was feast food; fish was plain fare
The fish was an early Christian sign
steps.why: Meat was the food of celebrations, and Friday, the day Jesus died, is no feast. Fish was everyday food, so it stayed on the table.

say: here’s what i love. the ash sounds grim, but catholics hear it as honest: you won’t be here forever, so what will you do with the time?
and giving something up isn’t a diet. each time you reach for it and stop, that empty space becomes a little room, for prayer, or for someone else. it’s the desert, in small.

steps.q: In the desert, Jesus said no to bread and no to every kingdom on earth. When a Catholic gives up something small for Lent, what is she doing?
o: Earning God’s love a little at a time
Keeping him company, and making room
Proving to herself how strong she is
steps.why: Catholics don’t believe you earn God’s love. Lent is company, not a contest: less, on purpose, so there’s room.

today.say: pick one small thing you reach for without thinking. today, when you catch yourself reaching, stop. use that pause for a short prayer, or a kind text to someone. your choice.
options: every reach becomes a reminder. that’s lent in one day.
noticing is the first step into the desert. that counts.

tomorrow.line: a woman in a crowd reaches out to touch one thing. he stops everything to find her.
